pr_title: Ensure we use the same provider as keymgmt where appropriate
pr_body:
To ensure that we get a signature, keyexch, etc method from the same
provider as the keymgmt of the passed pkey, we add functionality to
fetch from a specific provider instead of all available providers.

This is much safer than to re-use the same properties and hope for the
best.

Properties are still passed, in case the provider implements the same
algorithm multiple times with different properties.

Fixes #16614

pr_comments: This is an alternative to #16711

> A test case would be useful.

You mean it's not enough with the calls in the diverse pkey inits?  Basically, available tests are already implicitly modified!

Our tests didn't detect either of the two bugs.
A regression test that catches them would be good.

Broadly this looks good but it does not currently address the first of the two bugs described in [this](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/issues/16614#issuecomment-930365376) comment from #16614, i.e.

> If we have an EVP_PKEY_CTX with a pkey in it from a given provider, and the keymgmt for that pkey does not support exporting the key, then any fetches associated with that EVP_PKEY_CTX should not return an algorithm that is in anything other than the same provider.

Note that related to this is the fact that the `pctx->keymgmt` is fetched fresh when you construct the pctx (using the supplied propq), which may not match the keymgmt in the pkey. Therefore in the case where the key manager for the pkey is unable to export then the calls to `evp_pkey_export_to_provider` in the various init functions will fail.

> Broadly this looks good but it does not currently address the first of the two bugs described in [this](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/issues/16614#issuecomment-930365376) comment from #16614, i.e.
> 
> > If we have an EVP_PKEY_CTX with a pkey in it from a given provider, and the keymgmt for that pkey does not support exporting the key, then any fetches associated with that EVP_PKEY_CTX should not return an algorithm that is in anything other than the same provider.
> 
> Note that related to this is the fact that the `pctx->keymgmt` is fetched fresh when you construct the pctx (using the supplied propq), which may not match the keymgmt in the pkey. Therefore in the case where the key manager for the pkey is unable to export then the calls to `evp_pkey_export_to_provider` in the various init functions will fail.

... and that is actually correct behavior.  The caller sets up the EVP_PKEY_CTX for the provider that it would like the *operation* to happen in, which may differ from the one the input pkey resides, and if it does, it implies an export, which may fail if the key resides in an HSM and is therefore not exportable.

I don't think that it's the right answer to turn around and basically treat the caller with a "screw you, I'll look over there instead".

We have debated this before.

> ... and that is actually correct behavior. The caller sets up the EVP_PKEY_CTX for the provider that it would like the operation to happen in, which may differ from the one the input pkey resides, and if it does, it implies an export, which may fail if the key resides in an HSM and is therefore not exportable.

The scenario from #16614 is that the propq sets a *preference* for a particular provider to be used but does not *prevent* another one from being used if the preferred provider is unsuitable for some reason. We must of course still respect the asked for propq. But we can do *both*, i.e. respect the propq *and* return the correct key manager. There is no conflict here.


>I don't think that it's the right answer to turn around and basically treat the caller with a "screw you, I'll look over there instead".

We are not doing that. It is a given that we must continue to respect the requested propq. But if the propq doesn't prevent us from returning the correct key manager then we can do both: use the correct key manager *and* respect the requested propq.

> We are not doing that. It is a given that we must continue to respect the requested propq. But if the propq doesn't prevent us from returning the correct key manager then we can do both: use the correct key manager _and_ respect the requested propq.

+1 to that. What I don't like on the Matt's patch is that he is adding the provider=xxx to the query. IMO we should have an internal fetch routine that just respects the propq but also has additional provider pointer parameter and it would try to match it if it is set (and fail if there is no possible match with the propq).

> What I don't like on the Matt's patch is that he is adding the provider=xxx to the query. IMO we should have an internal fetch routine that just respects the propq but also has additional provider pointer parameter and it would try to match it if it is set (and fail if there is no possible match with the propq).

Yes, I agree that is a better approach. We probably need something somewhere between @levitte's patch and mine.

> > ... and that is actually correct behavior. The caller sets up the EVP_PKEY_CTX for the provider that it would like the operation to happen in, which may differ from the one the input pkey resides, and if it does, it implies an export, which may fail if the key resides in an HSM and is therefore not exportable.
> 
> The scenario from #16614 is that the propq sets a _preference_ for a particular provider to be used but does not _prevent_ another one from being used if the preferred provider is unsuitable for some reason.

In the SSL library, I completely agree.  With functions like `EVP_PKEY_CTX_new_from_pkey()`, I *disagree*.  That function doesn't set a preference, it sets what the caller demands, unconditionally...  or that was part of the design.

I think that we need to look at how `EVP_PKEY_CTX_new_from_pkey()` is used in the SSL library.  If we want to make a preference for the provider of caller supplied keys, that's the better spot to do so, in my opinion.
Do note that we're missing one or two getters to be able to do so, but that should be possible to add.
I intend to look more closely at that idea this evening.

> With functions like EVP_PKEY_CTX_new_from_pkey(), I disagree. That function doesn't set a preference, it sets what the caller demands, unconditionally... or that was part of the design.

Yes it *does*. In the propq you can explicitly set a preference and that is passed to EVP_PKEY_CTX_new_from_pkey()!!!

> I think that we need to look at how EVP_PKEY_CTX_new_from_pkey() is used in the SSL library. If we want to make a preference for the provider of caller supplied keys, that's the better spot to do so, in my opinion.

That is completely the *wrong* place to do it IMO!

Additionally, even if you don't set a preference in a propq, a propq may actually end up in multiple implementations becoming eligible for fetch. It is undefined which one eventually gets used. There is no problem with us additionally specifying that, once you have that set of eligible implementations, return the one that is in the correct provider.

> Consider this code:
> 
> ```
> /* Load the key from "myprovider". Key is unexportable. */
> EVP_PKEY *pkey = load_my_pkey("provider=myprovider");
> 
> /* Set a preference for the default provider, but allow others to be fetched if necessary */
> EVP_PKEY_CTX *pctx = EVP_PKEY_CTX_new_from_pkey(NULL, pkey, "?provider=default");
> 
> EVP_PKEY_sign_init(pctx);
> ```
> 
> This will fail currently due to the _bug_ noted above (there is no reason why this should not work), but has nothing to do with libssl. Fixing this in libssl will not fix the underlying problem.

Actually, this puts the spotlight on yet another thing that we've mentioned once or twice but not yet tackled: the matter of property weight.  "?provider=default" puts more *weight* on methods that have this property, and there is no way to specify that a certain property should be used as a last resort if nothing else is found.

> What would you expect, as a user that has just read the documentation?

I would expect the key to be generated in a provider that doesn't support asm. Then I would expect the signature operation to be fetched from a provider that does support asm, and the key to be exported from one provider to the other, and for the operation to succeed. If the key gen provider doesn't support export, then I expect the signature operation to fail. And? All of this still works the same way with the proposed solution.

> If the key gen provider doesn't support export, then I expect the signature operation to fail. And? All of this still works the same way with the proposed solution.

That is exactly what the existing code is supposed to do already, with the changes in this PR.

> That is exactly what the existing code is supposed to do already, with the changes in this PR.

We seem to be going around in circles here.....this PR is not sufficient to address the other bug!

I think this comes down to how we think about "preference", and where the signature algorithm comes from.

It may be that we have a different understanding of what the propquery "?provider=default", means.  Given these choices:

- a signature implementation with the property "provider=myprovider"
- a signature implementation with the property "provider=default"

...  I would expect that the latter would *always* be chosen, because that's the preference I indicated, and it has a signature implementation with the name I'm asking for.  That's what existing code does, isn't it?

What I'm hearing is that *if* the given key lives in a different provider and *if* it can't exported, then we must get a signature from the same provider as the key instead of what the caller asked to have fetched (given the choices above).  Have I finally been able to express the problem you're talking about correctly?

I'd say that this PR does solve one issue, the uncertainty of fetching keymgmt and operation implementation.

As @mattcaswell, the issue of what "preference" means in actual behavior should probably be fixed in a separate PR.

> ... I would expect that the latter would _always_ be chosen, because that's the preference I indicated, and it has a signature implementation with the name I'm asking for. That's what existing code does, isn't it?

That's an interesting interpretation and one that plausibly might be correct. But in that case we would need a different way how to  indicate that some provider should never be chosen unless there is no other choice. I.E., would have to have a method how to ensure that a special private key signing-only handling provider is never chosen for anything over (default/fips/...) unless I have specified `provider=my.special.provider` in the query. AND given the export would fail for the key it would try to fallback to implementation in the provider for any operation with the key.
I've updated #16711 to incorporate all the commits from here.

> I've updated #16711 to incorporate all the commits from here.

Bad move...  I'm about to do a take 2
CI failures look relevant

> To ensure that we get a signature, keyexch, etc method from the same provider as the keymgmt of the passed pkey, we add functionality to fetch from a specific provider instead of all available providers.
> 
> This is much safer than to re-use the same properties and hope for the best.
> 
> Properties are still passed, in case the provider implements the same algorithm multiple times with different properties.
> 
> Fixes #16614

Fixes what in #16614? Unlike claimed here, this does not fetch signature from the same provider as the keymgmt of the passed pkey. Instead, it continues to fetch it from the keymgmt of the passed EVP_PKEY_CTX which often the user has no control over (say created through SSL_CTX).  And then it continues to insist on exporting the key into it even when key is not exportable. To add to that, when keyexch is not implemented in the same provider as the key,  it continues to refuse to export the key into the keyexch provider even when key is exportable.

The issues reported #16614 is opposite: (i) key operations are not tied to the key even when key is not exportable (ii) working around (i) in TLS by creating SSL_CTX with a propq preferring the provider leads to the requirement of implementing keyexch in the provider. In a provider that just wants to do signature operation for an opaque key, this (or even generating keys) is a ridiculous requirement, IMO.  None of that is changed by this PR.

I am very strongly of the same opinion as @mattcaswell here.  An optional property can never be considered a mandate.  Given a choice between _has the optional property but doesn't work_ and _doesn't have the optional property and does work_, the choice should **always** be the latter.  At least with the caveat that we could reasonably know the former doesn't work as is the case here.
I'm going to drop this in favor of another upcoming PR.  This didn't target the right thing.

issue_context.title: Cannot use key and ciphers in different providers
issue_context.body:
For an external key (non-exportable) I use a custom provider with a minimal store, keymgmt and signature implemented. This works, the key can be loaded, and signing using EVP_PKEY_sign() calls the method in my provider. The latter requires the EVP_PKEY_CTX  created with the same propq as the key, though.

Now, to use the corresponding certificate in TLS, I create SSL_CTX in default context so that cipher and digest algorithms are available. And load the key as the private key. This errors during signature as it wants to export the key which is not possible. Is there a way out of this?

An edited snippet of the relevant code:
```
OSSL_PROVIDER_load(libctx, "ovpn.xkey");

EVP_PKEY *pkey = my_custom_loader(libctx, "provider=ovpn.xkey", uri); /* this loads an opaque pointer as keydata */ 

SSL_CTX *ctx = SSL_CTX_new_ex(NULL, NULL, method); /* using default context */
SSL_CTX_use_certificate(ctx, cert);
SSL_CTX_use_Privatekey(ctx, pkey);
..
```
In this case, all is good until  signature is needed which fails with calls to provider's keymgmt_export() with PRIVATE_KEY in selection, not possible for the key. So, it looks like the sign op is tried in the context for SSL_CTX which needs the key exported. 

If I use `SSL_CTX_new_ex(libctx, "provider=ovpn.xkey", method)` it fails quickly with "library has no ciphers".  Is it possible to get the sign operation called in the context of the key's provider, without losing access to algorithms in the default provider?
comments:
> If I use SSL_CTX_new_ex(libctx, "provider=ovpn.xkey", method) it fails quickly with "library has no ciphers"

Try:

````
SSL_CTX_new_ex(libctx, "?provider=ovpn.xkey", method)
````
This will prefer algorithms from your custom provider over algorithms from other providers. Of course you need to ensure that `libctx` also has the default provider loaded into it.

Thanks a bunch. Much appreciated. Prefixing with "?" resolves cipher/digest algs from default, and gets into sign in the right context.

And that has exposed some holes in my provider -- it now imports peer's public key into "ovpn.xkey" and needs support for digest_verify functions. I was hoping to get away with private key related ops only. Although most of it is copy paste, this is already ~1000 lines and growing. All just to replace a few lines of code using hooks into EVP_PKEY_METHOD (or engine). 

A built-in shim provider that would require only private key ops implemented would greatly help application authors who have to support a variety of "external" keys.

I think a proper solution would be to have a way to indicate finer granularity of algorithm support to the libcrypto from a provider. I.E., libcrypto would know that your provider supports only sign but no verify operations and would use the default provider instead. Of course that is a possible future feature, not something that can and will be done in 3.0.

For now you can open a child library context inside your provider and simply forward the operations to the default provider via that context. Of course that would still require having and import function for the public key to be implemented and it is not a completely trivial workaround.

One improvement could be to use the key's keymgmt to determine which provider's sign/verify ops should be called for it. Currently the signing context is determined by EVP_PKEY_CTX which is fine when the application creates it. With SSL_CTX created with some propq, it delegates all signature operation to the provider matching that propq irrespective of the key. When the key's keymgmt belongs to some other provider, this leads to the import/export process. And the need to implement DigestVerify which could have been directly handled by the internal default provider. Of course we only need to write some  glue for this,  but more code means more bugs.

Also allowing to leave out DigestSignInit and DigestSign to indicate that we prefer prefer SignInit and Sign would be nice. I thought that would be the case, but leaving them out leads to error.  This requires implementation of Digest in the provider as not all HSM's can do it internally (again, we can call OpenSSL back). Unless I missed some way of avoiding that.

Thanks for the pointers and help. My provider is working and I can get a TLS session established. But when the provider is loaded groups secp256r1, secp512r1 and secp384r1 disappears from the list in extension 10. That breaks ECDH with RSA. I have RSA and EC implemented in keymgmt and query_keymgmt_name returns "RSA" or "ECDSA" for sign-operation, NULL otherwise. I haven't implemented keyexch assuming it will be resolved from default. 

The application is OpenVPN client, and without the provider all is fine. Is there any reason why this would happen? I'm loading using propq = "?provider=ovpn.xkey" and have default provider loaded. Normally we do not use SSL_CTX_set1_groups unless the user wants to override it. And explicitly setting something like prime256v1, just makes extension 10 disappear. So something is removing/forbidding those groups only when the provider is loaded.

To add to that, here is what the client-hello has when traced from client side (the above was from what the server)

Using default provider only

```        
        extension_type=supported_groups(10), length=22
          ecdh_x25519 (29)
          secp256r1 (P-256) (23)
          ecdh_x448 (30)
          secp521r1 (P-521) (25)
          secp384r1 (P-384) (24)
          ffdhe2048 (256)
          ffdhe3072 (257)
          ffdhe4096 (258)
          ffdhe6144 (259)
          ffdhe8192 (260)
```
Using custom provider which overrides keymgmt and signature
```
        extension_type=supported_groups(10), length=22
          ecdh_x25519 (29)
          ecdh_x448 (30)
          ffdhe2048 (256)
          ffdhe3072 (257)
          ffdhe4096 (258)
          ffdhe6144 (259)
          ffdhe8192 (260)
```

If your provider is supplying groups to be advertised in TLS then it needs to tell libssl about them using the "TLS-GROUPS" capability. See the "provider_get_capabilities" function and the "CAPABILITIES" section on this page:

https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/master/doc/man7/provider-base.pod

Also see how the default and fips providers handle this here:

https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/master/providers/common/capabilities.c

I did a quick test by obtaining the list of capabilities in the default provider and returning that list. Not sure whether that's correct to do.

Anyway, that fixes ClientHello, server now responds with certificate which is fine and then ECDHE key exchange -- that fails:
```
error:03000096:digital envelope routines::operation not supported for this keytype
error:0A00013A:SSL routines::unable to find ecdh parameters
```
Looks like I need to implement something more. At the end of the day the only thing OpenSSL cannot access directly is the private key and the purpose of the provider is to interface with the backend and supply private key ops. Everything else, either I don't want my provider be called or I want to delegate back to the default provider.
It looks clear to me that in 3.1 we need to be provide a better way of saying - its the same as that algorithm but with these differences, e.g. some kind of "filter" provider.

I will get back to that "filter part" . Actually we only need a couple of groups by default and any custom ones that the user may provide as an option.

But it seems I have to implement EC key generation capability in the keymgmt. Kind of obvious in retrospect. I added a some empty code for gen_init, gen_set_params and gen and that is getting called. I was hoping that can avoid that... I can construct the EC key using default provider, so its not a big deal -- a lot more of glue code...

> It looks clear to me that in 3.1 we need to be provide a better way of saying - its the same as that algorithm but with these differences, e.g. some kind of "filter" provider.

Obviously.. please spare us of the kind of unnecessary pain I'm going through. Its good to get used to the innards of provider interface though :)

Now, how to delegate  EC key generation back to the default provider? Having never used keygen/paramgen, not sure what functions correspond to `keymgmt_gen_init`, `get_set_param` and `gen`. Here is what I tried as a shot in the dark, and that completes without error, but is it right?

In keymgmt_gen_init()
```
    EVP_PKEY_CTX *ctx = EVP_PKEY_CTX_new_from_name(prov->libctx, "EC", NULL);
    EVP_PKEY_CTX_set_params(ctx, p);
    EVP_PKEY_keygen_init(ctx);
```

The ctx is saved and passed on.

In keymgmt_gen_set_params()
```
EVP_PKEY_CTX_set_params(ctx, p)
```
Finally in keymgt generate
```
    EVP_PKEY *pkey = NULL;
    EVP_PKEY_generate(ctx, &pkey);
```

also need `set_template`, where I just used `EVP_PKEY_get_group_name` as I have the generated key hidden in the  keydata, and set it on the context using  `EVP_PKEY_CTX_set_group_name`. Is there anything else in the template?

At that point it queries keymgmt operation_name with OP_KEYEXCH where I return "ECDH". Then it wants keyexch implemented. I thought it will export the key out and use keyexch in default.

Anyway, I implemented keyexch using calls to `EVP_PKEY_derive` family of functions and all look good on surface. But the server rejects with "Verification of message MAC failed".  So something is not right.

Hmm. This latest difficulty with key gen and tls groups etc seems related to key exchange (ECDH) - not signatures (ECDSA). I'm wondering why you need to go into this - since your original problem was about signatures. Can you not use your own provider for signatures, and the default provider for key exchange?

Yes, signature is the only thing I want to provide. SSL_CTX is taking ciphers, rand etc from default but it seems a whole lot of ops are tied to keymgmt ~keyexch~ and there is no way to say call me only for signature.

Here is a summary of this thread:

If I create SSL_CTX in default context, then it wants to export the signing private key which is not possible. If I create SSL_CTX with "?provider=foo", then it always makes EVP_PKEY_CTX in the context of foo's keymgmt, and all operations including peer's public key ops, EC key generation for ECDH  are being done through foo's keymgmt. 

Now, if I generate EC key  through my provider it queries it for OP_KEYEXCH and errors if I don't return "ECDH". Once I return that it looks for keyexch in my provider. (I may be able to avoid keyexch by allowing to export the generated key -- I haven't tried as yet, as I'm stuck at proper key generation.)

I'll be more than happy not having to intercept all those calls.
Hmmm. This doesn't seem right. You should not have to implement KEYEXCH just because you have implemented SIGNATURE.

> Hmmm. This doesn't seem right. You should not have to implement KEYEXCH just because you have implemented SIGNATURE.

I think this is what happens: the propq passed to SSL_CTX_new...() is used by it for all fetches. It finds everything from default except keymgmt and signature from me. But when it ceates EVP_PKEY_CTX for EC key generation (for ECDH), the context's keymgmt is my provider. So it asks me to generate the EC key.  If I can avoid that, the question about keyexch is moot.

What is needed is a more fine-grained fetching. Like, if a keymgmt does not implement gen_init, gen_set_params and gen, take it from the next provider matching the propq. But it looks not possible in the current implementation of provider interface. Same with signature -- it should be possible to take DigestSign and Sign from one provider and DigestSignVerify and SignVerify from another.

> Now, if I generate EC key through my provider it queries it for OP_KEYEXCH and errors if I don't return "ECDH". Once I return that it looks for keyexch in my provider. (I may be able to avoid keyexch by allowing to export the generated key -- I haven't tried as yet, as I'm stuck at proper key generation.)

This *should* be the case, i.e. if you are able to export the generated key, then it should export it and import it into some other provider that *is* able to do keyexch.

> I think this is what happens: the propq passed to SSL_CTX_new...() is used by it for all fetches. It finds everything from default except keymgmt and signature from me. But when it ceates EVP_PKEY_CTX for EC key generation (for ECDH), the context's keymgmt is my provider. So it asks me to generate the EC key. 

This sounds plausible. Hmm. I can't think of a way around this at the moment.

> What is needed is a more fine-grained fetching. Like, if a keymgmt does not implement gen_init, gen_set_params and gen, take it from the next provider matching the propq. 

Yes - agreed we do need to be able to do this. Additionally we should be able to do this on a "group" basis, i.e. if you want P-384 but the fetched keymgmt only does P-256 then keep looking until you find a keymgmt that can do this.

Sounds like we should wait for 3.1 or 3.2 before we try to remove all deprecated API calls..

> > Now, if I generate EC key through my provider it queries it for OP_KEYEXCH and errors if I don't return "ECDH". Once I return that it looks for keyexch in my provider. (I may be able to avoid keyexch by allowing to export the generated key -- I haven't tried as yet, as I'm stuck at proper key generation.)
> 
> This _should_ be the case, i.e. if you are able to export the generated key, then it should export it and import it into some other provider that _is_ able to do keyexch.

I have a question on this. Once the key is generated it queries keymgmt_operation_name with id = OP_KEYEXCH (I know this because I made a bogus EC key for testing and tried to proceed). If I respond ECDH there, it expects to find keyexch with that name in the  the same provider. What else can I return here --- if I go by the docs, returning NULL would mean it would take the name to be same as that of the key ("EC") and expect the operation with that name implemented in the same provider.

So it seems keyexch is also tied to keymgmt?  (I'll do more tests and see).

In any case, hoping that the granular approach you mention gets implemented in future versions.

> it expects to find keyexch with that name in the the same provider.

This is actually quite surprising. I would expect it to export the key automatically to the right provider. I think there is a bug somewhere here....need to look, but I won't get time today.

My understanding of OpenSSL code base is poor to put it mildly, so take all of the below with a grain of salt (I stepped through it in debugger to confirm, though).

For ECDHE, `SSL_derive()` calls `EVP_PKEY_derive_init()` with a context created with the generated EC key and propq of SSL_CTX. So, this `EVP_PKEY_CTX` will have my provider's keymgmt in it. I refer to this context as `ctx` below.

Now, in `EVP_PKEY_dervive_ex_init()` in `crypto/ev/exchange.c` where that call lands, an export is attempted (line 233), but that's to the keymgmt of the `ctx`. Which is a no-op as the key is from there. At this point it doesn't know where exchange ops (keyexch) are going to come from. It does a `query_operation_name` (line 246) on the ctx->keymgmt which lands in my provider an I return "ECDH". 

That seems to be fine as it still fetches keyexch using that name "ECDH" and finds it in default provider (see around line 260 of `exchange.c`)

So far so good except for the fact that the key is still in my provider and exchange ops are in default. Then there is a check whether the provider of exchange matches that of the `ctx->keymgmt`. That obviously fails. 

```
260         exchange = EVP_KEYEXCH_fetch(ctx->libctx, supported_exch, ctx->propquery);
```

It finds exchange in default provider as I don't implement it.

```
261
262         if (exchange == NULL
263             || (EVP_KEYMGMT_get0_provider(ctx->keymgmt)
264                 != EVP_KEYEXCH_get0_provider(exchange))) {
265             /*
266              * We don't need to free ctx->keymgmt here, as it's not necessarily
267              * tied to this operation.  It will be freed by EVP_PKEY_CTX_free().
268              */
269             EVP_KEYEXCH_free(exchange);
270             goto legacy;
271         }
```

It goes to legacy and errors out as the key is not legacy.

It looks like a design decision to always export to the provider of `ctx->keymgmt` instead of to the provider of the operation.
Hmm, there is actually no way to fetch a keymgmt associated with the provider from the exchange method. IMO we need that function.

> It looks like a design decision to always export to the provider of `ctx->keymgmt` instead of to the provider of the operation.

I would not call it a design decision, I'd call it a mistake. If I am able to fetch the operation why not export the data to the provider of the operation.

> > it expects to find keyexch with that name in the the same provider.
>

I think there are two problems that I think are probably bugs in 3.0 which we probably can fix:

1) If we have an EVP_PKEY_CTX with a pkey in it from a given provider, and the keymgmt for that pkey does not support exporting the key, then any fetches associated with that EVP_PKEY_CTX should not return an algorithm that is in anything other than the same provider.

2) Having fetched an algorithm for use in an EVP_PKEY_CTX (e.g. a KEYEXCH), then we should always ensure that the keymgmt is in the same provider, and update the keymgmt in the EVP_PKEY_CTX if it is not.

These two are subtly different, but closely related.

If we fix these two things then I think it goes a long way to solving @selvanair's problems (you would not need to implement keygen, or anything to do with keyexch, or tls capabilities). ~~You probably would still need to handle the keymgmt_operation_name with id = OP_KEYEXCH thing though.~~

Basically if we fixed those bugs then you could fetch the key as now:

````
EVP_PKEY *pkey = my_custom_loader(libctx, "provider=ovpn.xkey", uri); /* this loads an opaque pointer as keydata */ 
````
And then setup SSL_CTX to prefer the default provider over yours:

````
SSL_CTX *ctx = SSL_CTX_new_ex(libctx, "?provider=default", method);
SSL_CTX_use_certificate(ctx, cert);
SSL_CTX_use_Privatekey(ctx, pkey);
````
Doing it this way, libssl would always use algorithms from default whenever possible. However the private key you loaded would have a keymgmt from your customer provider, and (with the bugs mentioned above fixed) then, because your provider cannot export, it would only fetch a SIGNATURE algorithm from your provider (overriding the preference in the propquery for the default provider). I think this even works for the verify stuff, i.e. when verifying you would not be using a key from your custom provider and therefore the SIGNATURE algorithm fetched would be from the default provider and therefore you should be able to get away without having to implement the verify code in your provider.

Unfortunately, we do not have the concept of "take it from the next one in line".  This was a design decision made very early (all the way back 3 years ago, when we started talking about the provider functionality), that a fetch simply gets you back one method, and if there are several choices, you get whatever comes first.

In retrospect, that design decision turns out to be a bit too blunt.
To be noted, thought, that there are "do_all" methods that iterate through all the methods given certain search criteria, called `EVP_{NAME}_do_all_provided()` (for example, `EVP_SIGNATURE_do_all_provided()`), which could be used for that sort of purpose.  It comes with a lot of churn, though...

Somewhere in the end, this appears to be a conflict of what the caller actually wants, and this comes all the way down to where operations are initialized.

So far, the priority has been that whatever the caller asks for rules.  If the caller has set up a key in one provider and has asked for the operation to happen in another provider, then that rules, and an export of the key to the operation provider *must* happen.

This does get complicated with the SSL library, where we may get a mix of different asks through different SSL functions.  I would rather think that the fix should be there, rather than making the EVP functionality less precise.

> one can get a pointer to it in provider init by calling OSSL_FUNC_core_get_libctx(in) 

What you get back from calling this function is an `OPENSSL_CORE_CTX` pointer. You are not supposed to cast this to an OSSL_LIB_CTX pointer. Probably the function name was badly chosen. There really should be some big red flashing warnings in the documentation about this. Actually there are some circumstances where you could get away with it and the world will not end (in particular where you are using built-in providers) - and in fact we "cheat" in the default provider and do exactly that (because we know it is built-in). But this is not documented and you really should not do it. Definitely not if you provider is not built-in.

The problem is that the definition of the OSSL_LIB_CTX type is opaque and cannot be guaranteed to be the same on both sides of the libcrypto <-> provider interface. It is entirely possible for the provider to be linked against a different version of libcrypto than the application. If that is the case then the definition of the OSSL_LIB_CTX type will be different on each side of the interface and bad things will happen.

> I suppose an application may have multiple libctx's and what is referred to here is the one used to init the provider, right?

Right.

Finally, the prop queries that I settled for --- in case others come across a similar predicament:

Assuming 16725 is merged, for my custom provider "ovpn.xkey" for unexprotable keys in OpenVPN, I use 
`?provider != ovpn.xkey` in SSL_CTX. The earlier plan based on discussions here was to use "?provider=default" but that assumes the user wants to use "default". Using of `!=` with `?` eliminates that guess work. 

I suppose this combination of `?` and `!=` is working not by accident and is indeed as designed.
